title: The Player-Coach Dilemma
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Opening with a cautionary anecdote about a top individual performer receiving a lukewarm review because their team never improved under them, this article examines the common failure mode of the 'player-coach': a strong individual contributor promoted to lead a team who keeps performing but neglects coaching responsibilities. It explains why this happens, since such leaders often believe their credibility rests entirely on personal output, and argues that balancing the two roles rarely means an even split, but rather deliberately allocating specific time and structure to team development. The piece recommends weekly check-ins and team-level goals as concrete fixes for player-coaches who default to only playing.
points: A cautionary anecdote: a top individual performer received a lukewarm review because their team never improved.
Player-coaches often default to pure performance because they believe credibility comes solely from output.
Balancing the roles rarely means an even split; it means deliberately allocated time for team development.
Weekly check-ins and team-level goals, not just personal goals, are recommended as concrete fixes.
quotes: You’re managing a team now, and you have responsibility to make people better. As a player-coach, you were excellent as a player and lousy as a coach.

The problem is that they often believe their credibility with the team and across the organization has little to do with their coach role and everything to do with their ability to perform at the highest level.
In practical reality, it is less likely for this to be a 50-50 percentage split, and more effective to pick days where one side of the role gets more time and attention.
Taking the time once a week to explore how each team member is doing and to listen to their concerns and challenges will turn a top player into a solid player-coach.
After all, no one refers to the role as coach-player for a reason.
